text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.
-- Partners in the Airbus consortium signed an agreement at the weekend to change the European aircraft builder into a corporation from a partnership by the end of 1999.

-- Education minister Francois Bayrou defends idea of apprenticeships which provide a diploma, advocated by some as a response to youth unemployment. Former prime minister Edouard Balladur calls for a minimum wage in such internships, saying the state should pay up to 20 percent of the pay involved.
-- Prudential Securities strategist Greg Smith expects higher trend to continue on Wall Street; Federal Reserve may cut rates if dollar remains strong.

-- Forecasts by 17 brokerage houses for 1997 see "improved company results, a pickup of economic growth and a possible surge of cash on the equity market". Brokers expect CAC 40 blue-chip index to reach 2.345,42 in three months from 2.237,50 last Friday.

-- President Jacques Chirac urges French people -- most of whom favour early retirement, according to a recent poll -- not to forget the economic difficulties of lowering the pension age. Balladur raises similar concerns at the weekend, saying retirement age should if anything be raised, not lowered.

-- Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer confirms he expects losses of automobile branch to continue through 1996 after a 991-million-franc loss in the first half, adds "our target for 1997 is a return to balance in the car division".

-- British media group United News and Media and French counterpart Havas sign agreement to create joint-venture company offering specialty broadcasting research and consultancy services to European media.
-- Project to introduce computer operations at the racecourse betting institution PMU may prove costly to its shareholders.
